strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question: whether SAM’s generalization gains carry privacy costs. Examining performance across examples with different influence profiles offers a useful perspective beyond aggregate accuracy.

Experiments cover four image and tabular datasets, multiple attack types, five randomized runs, and additional architectures. Several settings support increased single-query leakage: on CIFAR-100, SAM raises test accuracy from 79.92% to 82.04% while increasing attack accuracy from 76.68% to 79.09%.

SharpReg is a simple optimization modification that substantially reduces the tested attacks. On CIFAR-100, single-query attack accuracy decreases from 76.68% with SGD to 59.64%, with a 4.06 percentage-point reduction in test accuracy.
weaknesses: The central mechanism is not established. Section 3 uses precomputed SGD influence scores to group examples, then interprets SAM’s improved performance on those groups as increased memorization. Influence and memorization are algorithm-dependent by definition; neither memorization under SAM nor the connection between individual examples’ memorization and leakage is directly measured. Better representation learning and differences in example difficulty remain plausible explanations.

The proposed entropy metric needs stronger validation. Normalization discards influence magnitude, and taking absolute values conflates helpful and harmful influences. Equation (3) is undefined when all influences are zero, yet Appendix C.1 assigns 2,153 test examples to the highest-entropy bucket by convention. Sensitivity to this convention, estimation noise, and bucket boundaries is missing. Validation is limited to CIFAR-100.

The privacy conclusions overgeneralize heterogeneous results. In Table 1, SAM lowers multi-query attack accuracy from 69.18% to 65.41% on CIFAR-100 and from 56.36% to 54.01% on CIFAR-10; Table 5 reproduces this direction across architectures. Purchase-100 has slightly lower test accuracy and a single-query attack increase smaller than the reported standard deviations. These results require an attack-dependent explanation rather than a general flatness–privacy claim.

The attack tables contain a material inconsistency. Table 3 reports 77.04% correctness-based attack accuracy for CIFAR-100 SGD, whereas Table 4’s 99.98% training and 80.30% test accuracies imply approximately 59.84% under balanced, representative evaluation using Equation (8). Member/non-member balancing is insufficiently specified in Appendix C. These values and possible column-label errors need reconciliation.

SharpReg’s additional regularizer lacks the claimed independent interpretation. For xi < 1, Equation (5) is Equation (4) with lambda replaced by lambda/(1-xi), multiplied by the positive constant 1-xi. Although Appendix C.4.1 acknowledges parameter redundancy, the paper still presents the added term as a distinct mechanism for preventing overfitting and replacing early stopping. Ablations controlling effective sharpness weight, learning rate, and weight decay are needed.

The practical advantage of SharpReg is insufficiently established. Table 4 shows SELENA achieving higher test accuracy and lower attack accuracy for both attack categories than the default SharpReg setting on CIFAR-100 and Texas-100. Comparisons against tuned early stopping and standard regularization at matched accuracy are missing. Computational savings could justify the method, but runtime and memory comparisons are not reported.

The evaluation is insufficient for the claimed exhaustive privacy assessment. It omits strong per-example likelihood-ratio attacks such as LiRA and true-positive rates at low false-positive rates, which are particularly relevant to vulnerable atypical examples. Repetitions are described around attack-data splits, leaving variability across independently trained victim models unclear. Using one SAM perturbation radius throughout further limits the generality of the conclusions.
